idiom_name: final class with private final fields, validating constructor and package-private helpers
implementation_notes: Java supplies the boundary with access modifiers clients never see: a `final` class with `private final` fields, validation in the constructor and helpers that are either `private` or package-private keeps every other model type out of its signature, and `final` stops a subclass added elsewhere from attaching semantics the class does not state. The class's public API is then its complete definition, which is exactly the pattern's goal; `package-private` helper classes work as the module boundary on the classpath, and with JPMS a package that is not exported is invisible outside the module. Java 16 records replace this boilerplate for data-carrying types; the hand-written class stays right for types with behaviour, identity or a framework-required shape.
pitfalls: `java.io.Serializable` publishes the field layout: a serialized standalone class freezes its internals and needs `serialVersionUID` discipline, so prefer explicit DTOs for wire formats.

A `public` class in an exported package is available to the whole world; without JPMS the only per-type boundary is `final` plus private members, and package-private helpers are the practical module boundary.
Mutable static state or a caching factory re-couples the type to the model's lifecycle and makes unit tests order-dependent.
Final fields are not enough for deep immutability: a mutable component (array, `List`) can still be changed through its own API, so copy defensively in the constructor.

variants.name: Record as the standalone value
variants.idiom_name: record with a compact canonical constructor
variants.implementation_notes: A record declares its state and the compiler generates accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`, so the class's meaning is exactly its component list: the type is implicitly `final`, cannot extend any class, its fields are `final`, and the API cannot later be enhanced by a subclass - the language itself enforces the standalone guarantee. A compact canonical constructor keeps validation inside the type, static factories express named construction, and JPMS can hide the package entirely. Use it for standalone values (Money, Percentage, typed identifiers); keep the hand-written final class when the type needs identity, behavioural inheritance or a framework-required mutable shape.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a component of mutable type (array, `List`) can still be changed through its own API, so the value illusion depends on the components' types.
A record can implement interfaces but cannot extend a class - designs that need polymorphism must use an interface plus implementations, not a record hierarchy.
`equals` includes the runtime type and all components, so using a record as a JPA entity, or anywhere a framework mutates fields, contradicts its equality contract.
Records are not JavaBeans: frameworks that expect getters named `getX`/setters or a no-argument constructor do not work with them unmodified.
